source_text: Συναχθήτω τὰ ὕδατα, καὶ ὀφθήτω ἡ ξηρά. Συνέλκε ται τὰ παραπετάσματα, ἵνα ἐμφανὴς γένηται ἡ τέως μὴ ὁρωμένη. Ἴσως δ' ἄν τις κἀκεῖνο πρὸς τούτοις ἐπιζητήσειε. Πρῶτον μὲν, διὰ τί ὃ κατὰ φύσιν ὑπάρχει τῷ ὕδατι φέρεσθαι πρὸς τὸ κάταντες, τοῦτο ἐπὶ τὸ πρόσταγμα τοῦ δημιουργοῦ ὁ λόγος ἀνάγει; Ἕως μὲν γὰρ ἂν ἐπὶ τοῦ ἰσοπέδου κείμενον τύχῃ τὸ ὕδωρ, στάσιμόν ἐστιν, οὐκ ἔχων ὅπου μεταρρυῇ· ἐπειδὰν δέ τινος πρανοῦς λάβηται, εὐθὺς ὁρμήσαντος τοῦ προάγοντος, τὸ συνεχὲς αὐτῷ τὴν βάσιν τοῦ κινηθέντος ἐπιλαμβάνει, καὶ τὴν ἐκείνου τὸ ἐφεπόμενον· καὶ οὕτως ὑπεκφεύγει μὲν ἀεὶ τὸ προάγον, ἐπωθεῖ δὲ τὸ ἐπερχόμενον· καὶ τοσούτῳ ὀξυτέρα ἡ φορὰ γίνεται, ὅσῳπερ ἂν καὶ τὸ βάρος ᾖ πλεῖον τοῦ καταφερομένου, καὶ τὸ χωρίον κοιλότερον, πρὸς ὃ ἡ ἐπίρρυσις. Εἰ οὖν οὕτω πέφυκε τὸ ὕδωρ, παρέλκοι ἂν τὸ πρόσταγμα τὸ κελεῦον συναχθῆναι εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν. Ἔμελλε γὰρ πάντως, διὰ τὸ κατάρροπον τῆς φύσεως, ἐπὶ τὴν πάντων κοιλοτέραν χώραν αὐτομάτως συνδίδοσθαι, καὶ μὴ πρότερον στήσεσθαι πρὶν ὁμαλισθῆναι τὰ νῶτα. Οὐδὲν γὰρ οὕτω χωρίον ἰσόπεδον, ὡς ἡ τοῦ ὕδατος ἐπιφάνεια. Ἔπειτα πῶς, φησὶν, εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν ἐκελεύσθη τὰ ὕδατα συνδραμεῖν, ὅπουγε φαίνονται πολλαὶ οὖσαι θάλασσαι, καὶ πλεῖστον ἀλλήλων τῇ θέσει διωρισμέναι; Πρὸς μὲν οὖν τὸ πρότερον τῶν ἐπιζητηθέντων ἐκεῖνό φαμεν· ὅτι μάλιστα μὲν σὺ μετὰ τὸ πρόσταγμα τὸ δεσποτικὸν ἐπέγνως τοῦ ὕδατος τὰς κινήσεις, ὅτι τε περιρρεπές ἐστι καὶ ἀστήρικτον, καὶ πρὸς τὰ πρανῆ καὶ κοῖλα φέρεται κατὰ φύσιν· πρὸ τούτου δὲ, πῶς εἶχε δυνάμεως πρὶν αὐτῷ τὸν ἐκ τοῦ προστάγματος τούτου ἐγγενέσθαι δρόμον, οὔτε εἶδες αὐτὸς, οὔτε ἰδόντος ἤκουσας. Νόησον γὰρ ὅτι Θεοῦ φωνὴ φύσεώς ἐστι ποιητικὴ, καὶ τὸ γενόμενον τότε τῇ κτίσει πρόσταγμα τὴν πρὸς τὸ ἐφεξῆς ἀκολουθίαν τοῖς κτιζομένοις παρέσχετο. Ἡμέρα καὶ νὺξ ἅπαξ ἐδημιουργήθη, καὶ ἐξ ἐκείνου καὶ νῦν ἀλλήλας διαδεχόμεναι, καὶ κατ' ἰσομοιρίαν διαιρούμεναι τὸν χρόνον οὐκ ἀπολήγουσι. 4.3 Συναχθήτω τὰ ὕδατα. Ἐκελεύσθη τρέχειν τῶν ὑδάτων ἡ φύσις, καὶ οὐδέποτε κάμνει τῷ προστάγματι ἐκείνῳ κατασπευδομένη διηνεκῶς. Τοῦτο δὲ λέγω, πρὸς τὴν ῥυτὴν ἀφορῶν τῶν ὑδάτων μοῖραν. Τὰ μὲν γὰρ αὐτόματα ῥεῖ, οἷον τὰ κρηναῖα καὶ τὰ ποτάμια· τὰ δὲ συλλογιμαῖά ἐστι καὶ ἀπόρευτα. Ἀλλ' ἐμοὶ νῦν περὶ τῶν ὁρμητικῶν ὑδάτων ὁ λόγος. Συναχθήτω τὰ ὕδατα εἰς συναγωγὴν μίαν. Εἴ ποτέ σοι ἐπὶ κρήνης ἑστῶτι ἄφθονον ὕδωρ ἀναδιδούσης ἔννοια ἐγένετο, τίς ὁ ὠθῶν ἐκ τῶν λαγόνων τῆς γῆς τοῦτο τὸ ὕδωρ; τίς ὁ ἐπείγων ἐπὶ τὰ πρόσω; ποῖα ταμεῖα ὅθεν προέρχεται; τίς ὁ τόπος ἐφ' ὃν ἐπείγεται; πῶς καὶ ταῦτα οὐκ ἐκλείπει, κἀκεῖνα οὐκ ἀποπίμπλαται; Ταῦτα τῆς πρώτης ἐκείνης φωνῆς ἤρτηται. Ἐκεῖθεν τοῦ τρέχειν τῷ ὕδατι τὸ ἐνδόσιμον. Κατὰ πᾶσαν ἱστορίαν ὑδάτων μέμνησο τῆς πρώτης φωνῆς, Συναχθήτω τὰ ὕδατα. Ἔδει δραμεῖν αὐτὰ, ἵνα τὴν οἰκείαν καταλάβῃ χώραν· εἶτα γενόμενα ἐν τοῖς ἀφωρισμένοις τόποις, μένειν ἐφ' ἑαυτῶν, καὶ μὴ χωρεῖν περαιτέρω. Διὰ τοῦτο κατὰ τὸν τοῦ Ἐκκλησιαστοῦ λόγον, Πάντες οἱ χείμαρροι ἐπὶ τὴν θάλασσαν πορεύονται, καὶ ἡ θάλασσα οὐκ ἔστιν ἐμπιμπλαμένη.
thought_title: Why God commanded the waters to gather
orientation: Basil is answering objections about God's command 'Let the waters be gathered' in Genesis 1:9, explaining why a command was needed for what seems natural to water.
pass_a_gloss: Let the waters be gathered, and let the dry land appear. The curtains are drawn together, so that what was previously not seen may become visible. Perhaps someone might also seek this in addition to those things. First, why does the account attribute to the command of the creator that which belongs to water by nature, namely to be carried toward the downward slope? For as long as water happens to lie on level ground, it is stationary, not having anywhere to flow away; but whenever it takes hold of some slope, immediately the leading part having rushed forward, the water continuous with it seizes the base of what moved, and the following water seizes that one's base; and so the leading part always escapes, and the oncoming part pushes; and the movement becomes swifter by as much as the weight of what is carried down is greater, and the place toward which the flow is directed is more hollow. If then water is by nature like this, the command ordering it to be gathered into one gathering would be superfluous. For it was going in any case, because of the downward tendency of its nature, to run together spontaneously into the most hollow region of all, and not to stop before the surfaces were made level. For no place is so level as the surface of water. Then how, he says, were the waters commanded to run together into one gathering, when many seas are seen to exist, separated from one another by a very great distance in position? To the first of the things sought, then, we say this: that especially you knew the movements of water after the master's command, that it is inclined to flow around and is unstable, and is carried by nature toward slopes and hollows; but before this, how it was in power before the course from this command came to be in it, you neither saw yourself, nor heard from one who saw. For understand that the voice of God is maker of nature, and the command given then to creation provided the sequence for the future to the things being created. Day and night were created once, and from that time even now succeeding one another, and dividing the time in equal portions, they do not cease. Let the waters be gathered. The nature of the waters was commanded to run, and it never grows weary, being urged on continually by that command. I say this looking toward the flowing portion of the waters. For some flow of themselves, such as spring waters and river waters; but others are collected and without outlet. But my account now is about the rushing waters. Let the waters be gathered into one gathering. If ever, standing by a spring that sends up abundant water, a thought came to you: who is it that pushes this water from the flanks of the earth? who is it that urges it forward? what are the storehouses from which it comes? what is the place toward which it is urged? how do these not fail, and those not become full? These things depend on that first voice. From there the water received the signal to run. In every account of waters, remember the first voice: Let the waters be gathered. They had to run, so that each might occupy its own place; then, having come to be in the appointed places, to remain by themselves, and not to go further. For this reason, according to the word of Ecclesiastes: All the torrents go to the sea, and the sea is not filled.

choices.why: Keeps the passive voice and the metaphor of veils being pulled aside to reveal what was hidden; 'curtains' preserves the image of the water as a covering.

choices.term: τὸ συνεχὲς αὐτῷ τὴν βάσιν τοῦ κινηθέντος ἐπιλαμβάνει, καὶ τὴν ἐκείνου τὸ ἐφεπόμενον
choices.english: the water continuous with it seizes the base of what moved, and the following water seizes that one's base
choices.why: Preserves the exact chain of agency: the continuous water seizes the base of the moved water, then the following water seizes the base of that one. The source order is maintained.
rejected: the water next to it takes the place of what moved, and the following water takes its place

choices.english: the voice of God is maker of nature
choices.why: Renders ποιητική as 'maker' to emphasize that God's command actively creates the natural order, not merely describes it.
rejected: the voice of God is creative of nature

choices.why: ἐνδόσιμον is a technical term for the starting signal or cue given to begin; 'signal' captures the sense of a command that initiates ongoing motion.
The rare adjective συλλογιμαῖος means gathered or collected, contrasting with flowing waters; 'collected' keeps the passive sense of waters that have been gathered into pools.
ἀπόρευτος means having no passage or outlet; 'without outlet' is literal and clear for waters that do not flow onward.

pass_b_english: 'Let the waters be gathered, and let the dry land appear' (Genesis 1:9). The curtains are drawn together, so that what was previously unseen may become visible. Perhaps someone might seek in addition this further point. First, why does the account attribute to the command of the Creator what belongs to water by nature—its movement toward a downward slope? For as long as water happens to lie on level ground, it is still, having nowhere to flow. But when it takes hold of some downward incline, when the leading water rushes forward, the water continuous with it seizes the base of the one that moved, and the following water seizes the base of that one. And so the leading water always escapes from under, while the water coming after pushes it on. And the flow becomes swifter the greater the weight of what is carried down and the deeper the hollow into which the influx runs. If water is like this by nature, then the command ordering it to be gathered into one gathering would be superfluous. For it was bound to run together of its own accord, because of the downward tendency of its nature, into the deepest region of all, and not to stop until its surface was leveled. For no place is as level as the surface of water. Then, someone says, how was the water commanded to run together into one gathering, when there are clearly many seas, separated from one another by great distances in their position? To the first of these questions we say this: you have come to know the movements of water after the Master's command—that it flows downward and is unstable, and is carried by nature toward slopes and hollows. But before that, what power it had before the course from this command was born in it, you neither saw yourself nor heard from anyone who saw. Understand that the voice of God is maker of nature, and the command given then to creation provided the continuity for what was created thereafter. Day and night were made once, and from that time until now they succeed one another and divide time in equal portions without ceasing. 'Let the waters be gathered.' The nature of the waters was commanded to run, and it never grows weary, urged on continually by that command. I say this with reference to the flowing portion of the waters. For some flow of their own accord, such as springs and rivers; others are artificially collected and without outlet. But my subject now is the rushing waters. 'Let the waters be gathered into one gathering.' If you have ever stood by a spring that sends up abundant water and wondered: Who is it that pushes this water from the flanks of the earth? Who urges it forward? What are the storehouses from which it comes? What is the place to which it hurries? How is it that these do not fail, and those are not filled up? All this depends on that first voice. From there the water received the signal to run. In every account of waters, remember the first voice: 'Let the waters be gathered.' They had to run, so that each might reach its proper place; then, having come into the appointed regions, to remain by themselves and go no further. For this reason, according to the word of Ecclesiastes, 'All the torrents go to the sea, and the sea is not filled' (Ecclesiastes 1:7).

problems.quote: the water continuous with it seizes the base of what moved
problems.source_quote: τὸ συνεχὲς αὐτῷ τὴν βάσιν τοῦ κινηθέντος ἐπιλαμβάνεται
problems.why: Misreads syntax: τὸ συνεχὲς is subject, 'the continuous water seizes the base'; 'of what moved' is wrong, it's 'the base of the one that moved'.
problems.fix: the water continuous with it seizes the base of the one that moved

problems.quote: Who is it that pushes this water from the hollows of the earth?
problems.source_quote: τίς ὁ ὠθῶν ἐκ τῶν λαγόνων τῆς γῆς τοῦτο τὸ ὕδωρ
problems.why: λαγόνων = 'flanks, sides' (of body/earth), not 'hollows'; 'flanks of the earth' or 'bosom of the earth'.
problems.fix: Who is it that pushes this water from the flanks of the earth?
problems.ruling: λαγόνων means 'flanks/sides', not 'hollows'; mistranslates spatial metaphor, misleading reader.

edits.old: the water continuous with it seizes the base of what moved
edits.new: the water continuous with it seizes the base of the one that moved

edits.old: Who is it that pushes this water from the hollows of the earth?
edits.new: Who is it that pushes this water from the flanks of the earth?

fixed: Corrected 'of what moved' to 'of the one that moved' to match the Greek syntax (τὸ συνεχὲς as subject, κινηθέντος as genitive of the one that moved).
Corrected 'hollows of the earth' to 'flanks of the earth' to match λαγόνων ('flanks, sides').

problems.quote: the leading water rushes forward at once, the water continuous with it seizes the base of the one that moved
problems.source_quote: εὐθὺς ὁρμήσαντος τοῦ προάγοντος, τὸ συνεχὲς αὐτῷ τὴν βάσιν τοῦ κινηθέντος ἐπιλαμβάνει
problems.why: Misreads syntax: 'τοῦ προάγοντος' is genitive absolute ('when the leading water rushes'), not subject of next clause. 'τὸ συνεχὲς αὐτῷ' (the water continuous with it) is subject of 'seizes'. English makes 'leading water' subject of both actions.
problems.fix: when the leading water rushes forward, the water continuous with it seizes the base of what moved

edits.old: the leading water rushes forward at once, the water continuous with it seizes the base of the one that moved
edits.new: when the leading water rushes forward, the water continuous with it seizes the base of the one that moved

fixed: Corrected: 'τοῦ προάγοντος' is a genitive absolute ('when the leading water rushes'), not the subject of the next clause; 'τὸ συνεχὲς αὐτῷ' is the subject of 'seizes'.

problems.quote: others are collected and without outlet
problems.source_quote: τὰ δὲ συλλογιμαῖά ἐστι καὶ ἀπόρευτα
problems.why: συλλογιμαῖα = 'collected by human effort/artificially collected' (not naturally); 'collected' loses the key contrast with αὐτόματα.
problems.fix: others are artificially collected and without outlet
problems.ruling: συλλογιμαῖα = gathered pools vs αὐτόματα; 'collected' loses natural/standing-water contrast.

edits.old: others are collected and without outlet
edits.new: others are artificially collected and without outlet

fixed: The source συλλογιμαῖά means 'collected by human effort/artificially collected,' contrasting with αὐτόματα ('of their own accord'). The English 'collected' loses this contrast, so I added 'artificially' to make the distinction clear.

dismissed.quote: the water continuous with it seizes the base of the one that moved
dismissed.why: Greek says 'the continuous [water] seizes the base for itself' (dative αὐτῷ = for itself), not 'of the one that moved'; misreads syntax.
dismissed.note: αὐτῷ goes with τὸ συνεχές ('continuous with it'), and τοῦ κινηθέντος goes with τὴν βάσιν, so the English parses the Greek correctly.
